newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: PAL expects to fly higher with new aircraft.
newsitem.headline: PAL expects to fly higher with new aircraft.

text.p: Flag carrier Philippine Airlines Inc is expected to post profits in 1998 or in 1999 after three years of mounting losses, company officials said on Tuesday.
The delivery of 36 new aircraft would boost PAL's bottom line in coming years and improve its operations, officials said.

"(PAL) is expected to return to profitability between 1998 and 1999 after losing in the past three years," chief financial officer Jaime Bautista told reporters after the company's annual stockholders' meeting.
Bautista said PAL was projecting a loss of "more or less two billion pesos ($76 million)" for the fiscal year ending March 31 this year.
The airline had earlier projected a smaller loss for the current fiscal year at 1.0 billion to 1.3 billion pesos.
In 1995/96, the company's losses widened to 2.18 billion pesos from 1.72 billion in the previous year.
"Because of the strike we did not meet out target," Bautista told reporters. "The strikes cost us 500 million pesos."
The airline was besieged with a series of strikes last year due to a dispute over wages. It later forged separate collective bargaining agreements with its three labour unions.

Officials said the delivery of two aircraft in December last year and another 14 this year would help the airline improve efficiency and erase a sloppy image which has led to a common revision of what PAL stands for -- Plane Always Late.

At the annual meeting on Tuesday, stockholders unanimously approved an increase in PAL's authorised capital to 20 billion pesos from 10 billion. Last year, the firm doubled its capital to 10 billion pesos.
"The new capital hike, the second in less than a year, effectively paves the way for the flag carrier's fast-tracking of a $4 billion modernisation and expansion programme," a PAL statement said.
Of PAL's pending orders for 34 aircraft, eight are from Boeing and the rest from Airbus Industrie. The fleet currently totals 56.
Officials said PAL's management was now in a stronger position because bickering over the airline's ownership had died down.
"The factions are there but they are now acting in unison," president Jose Antonio Garcia said.
PAL is controlled by beer and tobacco magnate Lucio Tan but this was resented by other minority shareholders who wanted to oust him.
Tan's shareholding was not very large at the start but he managed to get control of the airline because all the other holdings, including the government's stake, were fragmented.
But late last year, the shareholders reached a deal under which they agreed to let Tan have control over the firm.
The settlement of the dispute made it possible for the company to go ahead with its much awaited modernisation programme. "It used to be wish list before," Garcia said. "Now it's concrete."
